2.text: to be intended for the use of “spirits,” when they approach and want to

3.text: “shake themselves;” that is, to beat the drum.

4.text: The beating of the drum, notwithstanding its seeming simplicity, requires

5.text: some skill, and the novice must spend considerable time before he can acquire

6.text: the desired degree of perfection. This has reference especially to the power

7.text: of endurance of the performer. The same may be said of the singing. The

8.text: manifestations continue for several hours, during all which time the shaman

9.text: exercises the most violent activity without scarcely a pause. After the per-

10.text: formance he must not show any signs of fatigue, because he is supposed to

11.text: be sustained by the “spirits;” and, moreover, the greater part of the exercise

12.text: is asserted to be the work of the “spirits” themselves, either while entering

13.text: his body, or while outside his body. The degree of endurance required for

14.text: all this, and the ability to pass quickly from the highest excitement to a

15.text: state of normal quietude, can, of course, be acquired only by long practice.

16.text: Indeed, all the shamans I conversed with said that they had to spend a year, or

17.text: even two years, before sufficient strength of hand, and freedom of voice, were

18.text: given to them by the “spirits.” Some asserted that during all this preparatory

19.text: time they kept closely to the inner room, taking up the drum several times

20.text: a day, and beating it as long as their strength would allow.

21.text: The only other means of training for inspiration, of which I am aware,

22.text: is abstention from all fat and rich foods, as well as great moderation in eating.

23.text: The same strictness is observed ever afterwards in the preparation for each

24.text: individual performance, in which the shaman tries to abstain wholly from food.

25.text: Various tricks performed by the Chukchee shamans, including ventrilo-

26.text: quism, have to be learned in the preparatory stage. However, I could obtain

27.text: no detailed information on this point, since the shamans, of course, asserted

28.text: that the tricks were done by “spirits,” and denied having any hand whatever

29.text: in proceedings of such a character.

30.text: In some cases, evidently, the old men have taught the younger genera-

31.text: tion, who are said to have received their power from them. The transfer is

32.text: final, and cannot be revoked. The man who gives a part of his power to

33.text: another man loses correspondingly, and can hardly recover the loss afterwards.

34.text: To transfer his power, the older shaman must blow on the eyes or into the

35.text: mouth of the recipient, or he may stab himself with a knife, with the blade

36.text: of which, still reeking with his “source of life” (tetkeˊyuñ), he will immediately

38.text: used by shamans in the treatment of their patients.

39.text: Most of the shamans I knew claimed to have had no teachers, but to

40.text: have acquired their art by their own individual efforts. I am not aware of

41.text: a single instance of the transfer of shamanistic power in the whole domain of
